kf1.tip: Choose a local shop you know and decide which internal source (retained profit, selling unwanted assets or owner's savings) could fund a new till, and why the others would not.
kf1.note: A good answer names one internal source and links it to the shop's situation. For an established shop, retained profit usually fits: it is free, with no interest and no repayment. Then say why the others fit less well. Selling unwanted assets only works if the shop owns something spare worth selling. Owner's savings put the owner's personal money at risk. A weak answer forgets that the shop must already have the profit, asset or savings.

kf2.tip: Imagine Tesco were a sole trader, not a plc. Say which source of finance it would lose, and which sources it would have to rely on instead.
kf2.note: Tesco would lose the ability to issue new shares, because only limited companies (Ltd and plc) can sell shares. As a sole trader it would have to rely on owner's savings, retained profit, loans, overdrafts and trade credit instead. If you named shares but left out what replaces them, you have only answered half the task. A strong answer notes these replacements mean borrowing or using money the business already has.

cs1.tip: Rank retained profit, selling unwanted assets and owner's savings from least to most risky for the owner, and defend each place in one line.
cs1.note: Most would put retained profit as least risky, because it is free and involves no repayment or loss of control. The only cost is less income for the owners this year. Selling unwanted assets comes next, because the asset cannot be recovered if needed later. Owner's savings are most risky, because the owner loses savings and income if the business fails. The trap is ranking by cost rather than by risk to the owner.
